data.text/markdown:
Verified data pipelines: a gentle introduction

You already know what a data pipeline is: read some tables, filter, compute new columns, join, union, and hope the result is right. This notebook explains what it means to prove that a pipeline (or a change to one) is right, using the Lean project in this repository. No prior knowledge of formal verification is assumed. Every idea comes with a small example you can play with. The roadmap
  1. A query is a plan: a tree of operators (Substrait).
  2. A plan has a meaning: an interpreter we agree to treat as the definition.
  3. A theorem is a claim about all inputs, not just the ones in your tests.
  4. Why NULL makes "obviously true" rewrites false.
  5. Well-formedness: the column-count bugs a checker can rule out.
  6. Incremental updates: refreshing a result from just the changed rows, provably.
  7. What is proven, and what is still trusted.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTests vs. proofs, in one sentence.\u003c/strong\u003e A test checks that your pipeline is right \u003cem\u003eon the data you tried\u003c/em\u003e. A proof checks that it is right \u003cem\u003eon every possible dataset\u003c/em\u003e, including ones with NULLs, duplicates, empty tables and values you never thought of.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
1. A query is a tree of operators

When you write 
SELECT id, amount * 2 AS doubled
FROM orders
WHERE amount > 10
a database does not run the text. It first turns it into a plan: a tree of small operators, each consuming the rows of its child. Substrait is a standard format for such plans, so DuckDB, DataFusion, Arrow and others can exchange them. Here is the plan for the query above, as Substrait actually writes it:

data.text/html: <marimo-mermaid data-diagram='"\n    graph BT\n      R[\"Read orders\u003cbr/\u003e(id, customer, amount)\"] --\u003e F[\"Filter\u003cbr/\u003e10 &lt; amount\"]\n      F --\u003e P[\"Project\u003cbr/\u003eappend amount * 2\"]\n      P --\u003e E[\"Emit\u003cbr/\u003ekeep columns 0 and 3\"]\n    "'></marimo-mermaid>

data.text/markdown:
Two Substrait quirks worth knowing, because the Lean model copies them:
  • Columns are numbered, not named. amount is just "column 2" (counting from 0). In Lean this is written $2.
  • Project only adds columns. It appends amount * 2 as column 3; a separate Emit step then keeps columns 0 and 3. So SELECT is really "Project, then Emit".

2. A plan has a meaning: the reference interpreter

To prove anything about plans, we first need to say precisely what each operator does. In Lean this is a function Rel.eval that takes a plan and the tables, and returns the result rows. It is written for clarity, not speed: it is the definition of correct, against which everything else is measured. Below is a line-for-line Python mirror of the Lean definitions, so you can see there is no magic. (The Lean versions are in SubstraitLean/Expr.lean and SubstraitLean/Rel.lean.)

data.text/html:
orders
idcustomeramount
1ada30
2bob5
3adaNULL
query(orders)
iddoubled
160

data.text/markdown:
Notice order 3 disappeared. Its amount is NULL, 10 < NULL is NULL ("unknown"), and a filter only keeps rows whose condition is true. Keep that in mind; it is the source of most surprises below.

3. What a theorem looks like

Optimizers constantly rewrite plans into faster, supposedly equivalent ones. A classic rewrite merges two filters:
Filter(Filter(r, p), q) ⟶ Filter(r, p AND q)
Here is how the Lean file SubstraitLean/Rewrites.lean states and proves it: 
theorem filter_filter (r : Rel) (p q : Expr) (cat : Catalog) :
    (filter (filter r p) q).eval cat = (filter r (.bin .and p q)).eval cat := by
  simp [eval, List.filter_filter, Expr.eval, BinFn.apply, isTrue_and3, Bool.and_comm]
How to read it:
Piece Meaning
theorem filter_filter the claim's name
(r : Rel) (p q : Expr) (cat : Catalog) for every plan r, every two conditions p, q, and every database cat
… .eval cat = … .eval cat both plans return exactly the same rows
:= by simp [...] the proof: unfold the definitions and simplify. Lean checks every step mechanically
The "for every" is the whole point. A test picks some r, p, q and some data; the theorem covers all of them, including tables with millions of rows you will never generate. The proof relies on one small fact, isTrue_and3: p AND q is true exactly when both p and q are true, even with NULLs. That fact only involves a handful of cases, so we can check every one of them right here, which is exactly what Lean's proof does (it splits into cases and checks each):

data.text/html:
pqp AND qkeep? (merged)keep? (two filters)same
truetruetruetruetrue✓
truefalsefalsefalsefalse✓
trueNULLNULLfalsefalse✓
falsetruefalsefalsefalse✓
falsefalsefalsefalsefalse✓
falseNULLfalsefalsefalse✓
NULLtrueNULLfalsefalse✓
NULLfalsefalsefalsefalse✓
NULLNULLNULLfalsefalse✓

data.text/markdown:
All nine cases agree, so the merged filter keeps exactly the rows the two separate filters keep. Lean checks the same nine cases, and then lifts the result to every table by reasoning about lists in general.

4. Why NULL breaks "obvious" rewrites

Here's a rewrite that looks harmless:
WHERE a = a ⟶ WHERE true (every value equals itself, right?)
It's wrong: NULL = NULL is NULL, not true, so the original query drops rows where a is NULL and the rewritten one keeps them. Testing finds this bug only if your test data happens to contain NULLs. Try it: generate random test tables and see how often the bug is caught.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003eThe bug was caught by \u003cstrong\u003e0 of 11\u003c/strong\u003e random tests.\u003cbr /\u003e\nWith no NULLs in the data, every test passes, and the bug ships.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"danger"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Lean can't be fooled this way. To claim the rewrite is correct you would have to prove (a = a) is true for every value of a, and the case a = NULL makes that impossible. The proof attempt fails, which tells you the rewrite is unsound before it ever reaches production.

The fine print: hypotheses

Some rewrites are only correct under conditions. For example, a filter can be moved below a Project (so fewer rows get the expensive new column), but only if the filter doesn't read the new column. Lean makes such conditions explicit as hypotheses: 
theorem filter_project_pushdown {cat : Catalog} (hcat : cat.WF)
    {r : Rel} {es : List Expr} {p : Expr}
    (hr : r.WF cat) (hp : p.refsLt (r.arity cat)) :
    (filter (project r es) p).eval cat = (project (filter r p) es).eval cat
  • hcat, hr: the tables and the input plan are well-formed (next section).
  • hp: the condition p only references columns that exist before the projection (refsLt = "all column references are less than").
Hypotheses are not a weakness. They are the precise conditions under which the optimization is allowed, written down where a machine can check them.

5. Well-formedness: ruling out column bugs

Since columns are numbered, a common bug is a reference to a column that doesn't exist: $5 on a table with 3 columns. The Lean project has a checker for this, and a proof (checkWF_iff) that the checker answers exactly the mathematical definition Rel.WF. The command-line tool substrait-check parses a real Substrait JSON plan, runs that checker, and evaluates the plan. Move the slider to change which column the filter in our query reads:

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='ROlb-0' random-id='02b3a138-1b83-b357-e8f8-27a1ea630366'><marimo-slider data-initial-value='2' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003efilter reads column $\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-start='0' data-stop='5' data-steps='[]' data-debounce='false' data-disabled='false' data-orientation='"horizontal"' data-show-value='true' data-include-input='false' data-full-width='false'></marimo-slider></marimo-ui-element>

$ substrait-check filter_project.json
Emit [0, 3]
  Project +[($2 * 2)]
    Filter (10 < $2)
      Read orders
tables: orders(3)
arity: 2
well-formed: yes
incremental: yes
roundtrip: ok

data.text/markdown:
Why does a proof about this checker matter? Because the main type-safety theorem, Rel.eval_arity, says:
If a plan is well-formed, every row it outputs has exactly the number of columns the plan declares.
So when the checker says yes, the theorem applies, and so do the rewrites that need well-formedness as a hypothesis.

6. Incremental updates: refresh from just the changes

Recomputing a big result every time a few rows change is wasteful. Incremental view maintenance computes only the change to the result from the change to the inputs. It's also easy to get subtly wrong. The trick that makes it tractable is to give every row a weight:
  • +1: this row was inserted,
  • −1: this row was deleted,
  • an update is a delete plus an insert.
A table with weights is called a Z-set. Adding a batch of changes is just putting the weighted rows together and summing weights per row. Pick some changes to orders:

data.text/markdown:
For this query the rule is simple: run the same query on just the changes, then add the result to the old one. That works because filter and project treat each row independently (they are linear). In Lean that is theorem Rel.zeval_add: 
theorem Rel.zeval_add : r.Incremental →
    (r.zeval (cat + Δ)).Perm (r.zeval cat ++ r.zdelta cat Δ)
Read: for every plan in the supported fragment, evaluating on the updated database gives the old result plus the delta (in some order: Perm means "same rows, possibly reordered").

Joins are trickier

A join pairs rows from two tables. If both tables change, the new result has four kinds of pairs:
old customers B new customers ΔB
old orders A A × B: already in the old result A × ΔB: new
new orders ΔA ΔA × B: new ΔA × ΔB: new, and easy to forget!
So the change to a join is ΔA × (B + ΔB) + A × ΔB. Forgetting the bottom-right cell is a classic bug in hand-written incremental pipelines. Toggle it off to see what goes wrong:

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='ZBYS-0' random-id='80332e5e-fc1a-e2b8-5c1c-147ef9369041'><marimo-switch data-initial-value='true' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003einclude the ΔA × ΔB term\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-disabled='false'></marimo-switch></marimo-ui-element>

Customer changes: insert cy (Lima), delete bob (Oslo). Order changes: as selected above.
incremental (old join + delta)
idcustomeramountnamecityweight
3adaNULLadaParis+1
4cy50cyLima+1
recomputed from scratch
idcustomeramountnamecityweight
3adaNULLadaParis+1
4cy50cyLima+1

data.text/markdown:
With the default changes, turning the switch off breaks the result in two ways:
  • the pair order 4 + customer cy is missing. Both are new, so only the corner term produces it;
  • phantom bob rows appear, one with weight −1: a row that "exists minus one times". The updated order 2 was paired with the old bob, and only the corner term cancels that pairing with bob's deletion.
Lean proves the full rule once and for all (ZSet.cross_add), and goes one step further: Rel.delta generates the delta plan automatically, as an ordinary plan that reads the old tables and the change tables, and Rel.delta_correct proves the generated plan computes exactly the change. Since the delta plan is an ordinary plan, a regular engine such as DuckDB can run it. The fragment covers filter, project, emit, union, cross and inner join. Left joins and LIMIT/OFFSET are excluded on purpose: a left join's NULL-padded rows must be retracted when a match shows up later, and LIMIT depends on row order. They need different rules.

7. What is proven, and what is trusted

A proof is only as good as what it is about. Here is the honest picture:

data.text/html: <marimo-mermaid data-diagram='"\n    graph LR\n      J[\"Substrait JSON\u003cbr/\u003e(from DuckDB, Ibis, …)\"] --\u003e|\"parser\u003cbr/\u003eTRUSTED · golden tests\"| M[\"Lean model: Rel\"]\n      M --\u003e|\"PROVEN\u003cbr/\u003erewrites, type safety,\u003cbr/\u003eincremental rules\"| M2[\"equivalent / delta plan\"]\n      M2 --\u003e|\"engine runs it\u003cbr/\u003eTRUSTED · differential tests\"| D[\"DuckDB result\"]\n      style M fill:#d4f4dd,stroke:#2e8b57\n      style M2 fill:#d4f4dd,stroke:#2e8b57\n    "'></marimo-mermaid>

data.text/markdown:
• Proven (green): everything about the Lean model Rel: the rewrites, type safety, the incremental rules. Lean checks these mechanically, and #print axioms confirms no step was skipped.
  • Trusted, guarded by tests: the JSON parser (does it translate the plan faithfully?) and the engine (does DuckDB behave like the model, e.g. on NULLs or integer overflow?). We compare against them with golden tests and, next, random differential tests.
This is the normal shape of verified systems: a small proven core, plus a clearly labelled trusted boundary that is tested hard.

data.text/html:
• Plan / relation (Rel): a tree of operators: Read, Filter, Project, Emit, Join, …
  • Semantics (Rel.eval): the reference interpreter that defines what a plan means.
  • Theorem: a statement quantified over all inputs, checked by Lean.
  • Hypothesis: a condition a theorem needs (e.g. "the filter only reads old columns").
  • Well-formed (Rel.WF): every column reference exists and union inputs agree on width.
  • Bag: a table where duplicate rows count; order doesn't matter.
  • Z-set: a bag where rows carry integer weights; negative means deleted.
  • Delta (Δ): the change to a table, or to a query result.
  • Linear operator: one that handles each row independently, so Q(A + ΔA) = Q(A) + Q(ΔA).
  • Perm: "same rows, possibly in a different order."
  • Trusted base: the parts not covered by proofs (parser, engine).

A good first exercise in Lean: in Rewrites.lean, try to prove filter_project_pushdown without the hypothesis hp. Lean will get stuck exactly where a filter reads a column that only exists after the projection.
